title: "No blame on you today"
hook: a grieving father who never despairs, a brother who forgives, and a shirt that brings back sight
carry: forgive one old thing, out loud
tomorrow: the vow and the fruit out of season

segments.voice: Yesterday, cup, the brothers at the gate: hungry, asking for grain, with no idea who was filling their sacks. Your line was he knew them. Did you manage one kindness toward someone who once hurt you? Day sixty-eight, the last day of Yusuf.

The brothers go home without the youngest, and the eldest stays behind in Egypt, unwilling to face his father. First Yusuf, years ago, and now his little brother too. Ya'qub turns away from them, and the Qur'an says his eyes went white with grief. His sons think he'll grieve himself to death. And he answers: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” Then, of all things, he sends them back. Go, he says, look for Yusuf and his brother, and “despair not of the Spirit of Allah.” So they return to Egypt a third time, poor, embarrassed, begging for a little grain as charity. And the powerful man across the table asks them a quiet question. Do you know what you did to Yusuf? They stare at him. Wait. Are you Yusuf?
screen: `A FATHER'S EYES GO WHITE.` → `DESPAIR NOT.` → `ARE YOU YUSUF?`

segments.voice: I am Yusuf, he says, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. They threw him in a well. They sold him for a few coins. They lied to their father with a shirt and false blood. He spent years as a servant and years in a prison. He holds the grain of Egypt, and they're standing in front of him with empty sacks. The brothers admit it: Allah has preferred you over us, and we were wrong. And Yusuf's answer, in Arabic, is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm. No blame on you today. No reproach, no scolding, no list of what you did. And then, may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of those who show mercy. He doesn't make them earn it. He doesn't wait for them to grovel. Then the shirt comes back into the story, one last time. The first shirt came home with false blood on it. The second was torn from behind and proved him innocent. Now Yusuf sends a third: lay this on my father's face. Before the caravan even arrives, Ya'qub says, I can smell Yusuf. The shirt touches his face, and he sees again. Finally the whole family comes to Egypt. Yusuf raises his parents up beside him, and they all bow down. And Yusuf says: “This is the interpretation of my dream of old.” Eleven stars, the sun and the moon, from the very first day of this story. Notice one more thing. When Yusuf tells the story back, he says Shaytan made trouble between me and my brothers. Even then, he won't name them as the villains. Muslims remember that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, years later, is reported to have answered his own old enemies in Mecca with these same words of Yusuf.
screen: `I AM YUSUF, AND THIS IS MY BROTHER.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `THE THIRD SHIRT: HIS FATHER SEES.` · `THE DREAM COMES TRUE.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE SPIRIT OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one old thing, out loud. Settle, and breathe. Let one old hurt come up, not the biggest one, just one that still stings a little. A friend who didn't show up. A sibling who said the wrong thing years ago. Picture their face. Then say it, quietly, out loud, just to the room: forgive one old thing, out loud. You don't have to feel it all the way. Today is enough. If you pray, you can ask Allah to forgive them, the way Yusuf did. The bell holds the time.
Tathrib, reproach: the word Yusuf set aside when he told his brothers, no blame on you today.

Your line: forgive one old thing, out loud. Once today, when someone apologizes, or should, let it go without the lecture. That's all fourteen days of Yusuf, from a dream to a dream come true. Tomorrow, Maryam's story begins. Day sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims often recall Yusuf's words to his brothers when making peace after a quarrel, and many read Surah Yusuf in full as a story of patience, trust and forgiveness.

match.prompt: what's inside the ending — tap the pairs.
pairs: the dream of old, come true

myth: Yusuf makes his brothers beg before he forgives them
his answer is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm: no blame on you today, and may Allah forgive you.
in the story, Ya'qub's sight comes back when Yusuf's shirt touches his face
Yusuf sends the shirt with his brothers; laid on his father's face, it restores his sight (12:93–96).
when he tells the story back, Yusuf blames his brothers for everything
he says Shaytan made trouble between him and his brothers (12:100).

fork.setup: Yusuf holds all the power now. the brothers who threw him in a well stand before him, poor and ashamed. what does he say?
options: list everything they did, one by one.
send them away without the grain.
fork.reveal: la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm: no blame on you today. may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful (12:92).

original.note: Arabic, Qur'an 12:92: no reproach on you today.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about letting it go.
what it means: Yusuf, holding all the power, refuses to scold the brothers who sold him, and asks Allah to forgive them.
what a scholar hears: tathrib is reproach, rebuking someone with their faults. tradition reports that the Prophet ﷺ echoed Yusuf's words when he forgave the people of Mecca.

notes: The index word is the full title in quotation marks ("No blame on you today"); kept exactly as the index has it.
Pickthall 12:86, 12:87 and 12:100 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording. 12:92 is paraphrased (Pickthall renders it roughly 'Have no fear this day!'; confirm and consider quoting).

Report that the Prophet quoted Yusuf's words ('I say to you what my brother Yusuf said') at the conquest of Mecca: found in seerah and in al-Bayhaqi's Sunan al-Kubra; strength of chain debated. Stated as 'is reported'. Confirm.

'Raises his parents up beside him' follows 12:100 ('raised his parents up on the throne'). Many commentators say 'parents' here includes his mother or his aunt/stepmother; the script says 'parents' without deciding. Confirm.
The prostration in 12:100 is understood by commentators as a bow of greeting/honor permitted in earlier law, not worship. The script says 'bow down'. Confirm whether a note is wanted.

Editor review 2026-10-01: the review said the brothers bowed at the gate; the Qur'an's arrival scene (12:58) has no bowing (that is Genesis), and the bow comes only at 12:100, so corrected. Hook now follows 12:80 (the eldest stays behind) and says 'the youngest' as day 67 does; 'most powerful man in the land' (unsourced superlative) and the invented tent cut.
